Sidebar

Layouts to copy

The Application shell guide has two whole layouts built from these parts, the sidebar layout and the header layout, and what every layout needs around them.

Built from parts

Section titled “Built from parts”

An application shell with a sidebar is four components, as in shadcn/ui:

  • <sl:sidebar-provider> wraps the whole page and holds the state: is the sidebar expanded or collapsed on a desktop.
  • <sl:sidebar> is the navigation itself: a <nav> landmark named “Main”.
  • <sl:sidebar-inset> is the page’s <main>, beside the sidebar: <main id="main" tabindex="-1">, the target of the skip link.
  • <sl:sidebar-trigger> is the icon button that collapses the sidebar, or opens it on a phone. It usually sits in a header at the top of the inset.

Put the sidebar straight inside the provider (not in an element of your own): the CSS that collapses it looks for it there.

The skip link comes first in the body: the sidebar puts many links before the content, and it lets a keyboard user jump past them to the inset. The header at the top of the inset holds the trigger, a vertical separator and the breadcrumb, as shadcn’s blocks have it. Lay it out as a row yourself, or use a site header, which does it for you, as the sidebar layout does.

What goes inside

Section titled “What goes inside”

The sidebar holds a header, the content and a footer, with shadcn/ui’s names:

  • <sl:sidebar-header> at the top (the application or team) and <sl:sidebar-footer> at the bottom (settings, help, later the signed-in user). They stay in view.
  • <sl:sidebar-content> between them, which scrolls when there is more than fits. It is a plain div: the sidebar itself is the navigation landmark.
  • <sl:sidebar-separator> draws a line between parts; screen readers skip it.

The content is made of groups, and each group of a menu:

  • <sl:sidebar-group> with a <sl:sidebar-group-label> is a group named by its label: a screen reader says “Platform, group” when the focus moves into it. The label’s id is the group’s id with -label; without an id the group generates one on every render. Without a label, a group is a plain div.
  • <sl:sidebar-group-content> holds the group’s menu, below the label.
  • <sl:sidebar-menu> is a list (ul), so a screen reader says how many entries it has, and <sl:sidebar-menu-item> one entry (li).
  • <sl:sidebar-menu-button> is the link: an icon in the icon-start slot (and icon-end for one at the end), then the label, which ends in an ellipsis when it does not fit. For two lines, put each in an element of its own, such as <strong> and <small>.

Menu buttons

Section titled “Menu buttons”

A menu button is a link (as="a", the default), or with as="button" a button, for an action that is no page of its own; every attribute that is no prop passes through, so hx-get or commandfor work as on any button. size is default, sm (a dense list, such as the footer’s) or lg (two lines, such as the application’s name in the header), and variant="outline" adds a background and a border. disabled works as on <sl:button>: a disabled link loses its href and leaves the tab order.

The current page

Section titled “The current page”

active marks the current page: the link gets aria-current="page", which a screen reader says (“current page”), and the accent background. A menu button that is a button gets aria-current="true" (“current”).

A layout usually has no model attribute saying which page it shows. #slNav.current(path) asks the request:

  • The path is the application’s own, as in @{/people}: a context path makes no difference.
  • It is the current page for /people and for every page below it, such as /people/12/edit, but not for /peoples. #slNav.current('/people', true) is only /people itself.
  • / is only the current page for / itself, or Home would be current on every page.
  • A query string and a trailing slash are ignored: /people?page=2 is /people.

On a phone the panel opens with the focus on the current page’s link. With hx-boost on the body every page comes from the server with the right link marked; an application that swaps only the main area leaves the old one marked, unless it swaps the menu too (out of band).

Badges

Section titled “Badges”

<sl:sidebar-menu-badge> puts a count at the end of a menu button, inside the same menu item:

The button is described by the badge (aria-describedby), so when Tab reaches it a screen reader says “Inbox, link, 12 unread”. label is what it says instead of the bare number. The badge’s id is the item’s id with -badge; without an id the item generates one on every render.

Actions

Section titled “Actions”

<sl:sidebar-group-action> is an icon button at the end of a group’s label (“Add project”), and <sl:sidebar-menu-action> one at the end of a menu item, beside its button (“More”). Both hold only an icon, so they need an aria-label; name the entry too, as every item has one (“More for Design Engineering”). With as="a" they are links. show-on-hover on a menu action hides it on a desktop until the pointer is over its item or the focus is in it; on a phone it is always there. On a phone both are 24 px, the minimum target size of WCAG 2.2.

Collapsible groups

Section titled “Collapsible groups”

A menu item with collapsible is a group of links that opens and closes, as shadcn’s sidebar-07 has: its menu button is what the user clicks, and <sl:sidebar-menu-sub> holds the links, indented along a line below it. It is the browser’s details element (the button becomes its summary, with a chevron that turns when it opens), so it needs no JavaScript, and the keyboard opens and closes it with Enter and Space.

  • open renders the group open. Open the one that holds the current page, so its link is in view: #slNav.current('/settings') is true on every page below /settings. When the pages share no path, combine them: th:open="${#slNav.current('/people') or #slNav.current('/teams')}".
  • <sl:sidebar-menu-sub-button> is a link (or as="button") like a menu button: active marks the current page, size is md (the default) or sm, disabled works as on a menu button, and an icon goes in icon-start.
  • The menu button of a collapsible item takes no href: it opens the group. Link the group’s first page as a sub-button.
  • A collapsible item takes no badge or action: the browser hides everything in a closed details but its summary. Put a count on a sub-button instead.

One element for a desktop and a phone

Section titled “One element for a desktop and a phone”

The server does not know how wide the screen is, so the sidebar is one element for both:

  • From 768 px (shadcn’s md) it is a column beside the page, as tall as the screen and sticky while the page scrolls. The trigger, or Ctrl+B (⌘B on a Mac), collapses it out of view and expands it again. A collapsed sidebar’s links leave the tab order.
  • Below 768 px it is hidden, and the trigger opens it as a panel over the page, with the page dimmed behind it. The focus moves to the current page’s link (aria-current="page") or the first link. Tab stays in the panel, and the rest of the page is inert, so a screen reader finds only the navigation. Escape, a click outside, Ctrl/⌘B, following one of its links and widening the window past 768 px close it, and the focus goes back to the trigger.

The sidebar is a popover (<nav popover>): the browser shows the panel in the top layer and closes it on Escape or a click outside, without script. On a desktop the CSS shows it in the page instead, where it is a plain navigation landmark.

Ctrl/⌘B does nothing while the focus is in a rich text editor (contenteditable), where it means bold.

<sl:sidebar-provider> has to start at the top of the page. On a desktop the sidebar is sticky at the top of the screen and as tall as the screen, so below a header of the page’s own (shadcn’s sidebar-16) it would slide under that header and run past the bottom of the screen. Put the page’s header inside <sl:sidebar-inset>, or the navigation in the header with placement="header".

The state is remembered

Section titled “The state is remembered”

When the user collapses or expands the sidebar, the browser stores the choice in a cookie, sl-sidebar-state (expanded or collapsed, for a year, the whole site). <sl:sidebar-provider> reads it on the server, so the next page renders in the same state from the first paint: nothing jumps, with or without htmx.

  • default-state="collapsed" starts collapsed until the user chooses.
  • state renders a state whatever the cookie says, for an application that keeps the choice itself, such as in the user’s settings: <sl:sidebar-provider th:state="${settings.sidebar}">. Listen to sl-sidebar-toggle (below) to save it.

The phone panel ignores the state: it always opens with everything in it.

Variants

Section titled “Variants”

variant changes how the sidebar looks on a desktop, as shadcn/ui’s:

  • sidebar (the default) is a column along the edge of the screen, with a border on the page’s side.
  • floating is a panel with a margin all round, rounded (in the vega skin) and with a shadow. It takes as much room as the plain sidebar, so a page lays out the same with either.
  • inset gives the sidebar no edge: its colour lies around the page, and <sl:sidebar-inset> becomes a card on it, with a margin, rounded corners (vega) and a shadow. The example at the top of this page, and the sidebar layout, use it.

Below 768 px the variant makes no difference: the panel and the page are the same for all three.

Collapsed to icons

Section titled “Collapsed to icons”

collapsible="icon" collapses the sidebar to a strip of its menu buttons’ icons instead of moving it out of view, as shadcn’s sidebar-07 does. It is as wide as --sidebar-width-icon (3 rem in both skins); floating and inset add their margin around it.

  • Every menu button becomes a square with its icon in the middle. The label is visually hidden, not removed: it stays the link’s name, so a screen reader still says “Inbox, link”. A large button (the application’s name in the header) loses its padding, so a logo as large as the square fills it.
  • Badges, actions, sub-menus and a collapsible item’s chevron are hidden. A badge still describes its button. Group labels move out of view but still name their groups.
  • tooltip on a menu button shows its label beside it, on hover and on keyboard focus, while the sidebar is collapsed to icons; never while it is expanded or on a phone. It repeats the button’s name, so it is hidden from screen readers and describes nothing (as a tooltip with mode="label"). Give every menu button one: without it, the icon alone has to say where the link goes.
  • A click (or Enter) on a collapsible group’s icon expands the sidebar and opens the group, as the sub-menu has no room in the strip. A group that holds the current page shows it on its icon.
  • The server renders the strip from the cookie, so the first paint is right with and without JavaScript. On a phone the panel ignores it and shows everything.

collapsible="offcanvas" (the default) moves the collapsed sidebar out of view. collapsible="none" never collapses it: the trigger is hidden on a desktop and Ctrl/⌘B does nothing there, whatever the cookie says. On a phone it is the panel, as with the other two.

Side

Section titled “Side”

side="end" puts the sidebar at the end of the line: the right, or the left on a right-to-left page (dir="rtl"). The default, start, is the left, or the right on a right-to-left page. The panel slides in from the same edge.

In the header

Section titled “In the header”

placement="header" puts the same <sl:sidebar> inside a <sl:site-header> instead of beside the page: from 768 px it is a row of links in the header, and narrower it is the panel, as in the sidebar layout. Nothing is rendered twice: it is one nav with one set of ids at every width. Inside <sl:sidebar-provider>, the header goes first and <sl:sidebar-inset> below it:

In the row the menu buttons show their labels only (no icons), the current page marked as in the sidebar. Groups run one after the other; a group’s label is visually hidden but still names it for a screen reader. Badges and actions stay beside their links. Collapsible items, group actions and separators are left out of the row: a sub-menu that drops down from a header is a different component (a navigation menu), which Shadleaf does not have yet. Mark such an item panel-only so it is still in the panel.

When the links do not fit, the row scrolls sideways (with a thin scrollbar where the system shows them), and a link the keyboard reaches scrolls into view; the page itself never gets wider. Keep the row short with panel-only parts.

The row never collapses, so collapsible, the cookie’s state and Ctrl/⌘B do nothing on a desktop, and the trigger is hidden there. Give the trigger a menu icon and a name of its own, as above: it opens the panel on a phone only. side still picks the panel’s edge. Of the variants only inset counts: the page becomes a card below the header, on the sidebar’s colour, as in the sidebar layout.

On a phone the menu button opens the same nav as the panel, with everything in it: icons, group labels, collapsible groups, and the panel-only parts.

Panel-only parts

Section titled “Panel-only parts”

panel-only on <sl:sidebar-header>, <sl:sidebar-footer>, <sl:sidebar-group> or <sl:sidebar-menu-item> shows it only in the phone panel: from 768 px it is left out (display: none). In the header placement it keeps the row short (favourites, Settings and Help in the examples above), and gives the panel a header of its own with the application’s name, which the site header already shows on a desktop. It works in the sidebar layout too, for an entry that is only needed on a phone.

Trigger

Section titled “Trigger”

The trigger is a ghost icon button with a panel icon (turned around on a right-to-left page), named “Toggle sidebar” (the message sl.sidebar.trigger). An aria-label replaces the name, and content of its own replaces the icon:

for points it at a sidebar with another id than sidebar. variant and size are the button’s (icon sizes only).

Motion

Section titled “Motion”

On a desktop the sidebar slides out and the page widens with it (collapsed to icons, it narrows to the strip and the group labels slide up); on a phone the panel slides in from its edge and the backdrop fades. With reduced motion (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) the changes are immediate.

Without JavaScript

Section titled “Without JavaScript”

The parts inside the sidebar need none: the current page, the badges and the actions are all in the markup (an action does what its attributes say), and collapsible groups are the browser’s details. Tooltips need it: without JavaScript a strip of icons shows none. The phone panel still opens and closes: that is the browser’s popover. It is not modal then (Tab can leave it), and it stays open when one of its links goes to a place on the same page. On a desktop nothing can collapse the sidebar, so the trigger is hidden there (@media (scripting: none)); the sidebar shows in the state the cookie asked for, also as a strip of icons, where a click on a group’s icon then opens a sub-menu the strip hides.

htmx

Section titled “htmx”

With hx-boost on the body, every page comes from the server with the sidebar in the cookie’s state, the current page marked and the panel closed. Boosting only the main area works too: following a link in the panel closes it, and a trigger htmx swaps in is set up again. Going back through htmx’s history shows the page with the panel closed (whether a popover is open is not part of the markup htmx saves, and the panel closes before htmx takes its snapshot), and in the state the user chose last: the snapshot holds the state of the moment it was taken, so the restored page reads the cookie, as the server would.

A boosted link sends HX-Request too. A controller that answers htmx with a fragment (a table’s rows, a dialog) must tell such a link apart, or the sidebar’s link to that page gets the fragment alone: a link the body’s boost sends has HX-Boosted and no HX-Target (the body has no id), and wants the whole page. The Application shell guide shows the check.

Left out

Section titled “Left out”

For now:

  • a collapsible group whose chevron is a menu action beside a link (shadcn’s sidebar-08), and sub-menus that open as dropdown menus while collapsed to icons (sidebar-06);
  • a menu action that opens a dropdown menu;
  • SidebarInput (use <sl:input>) and SidebarMenuSkeleton (use <sl:skeleton>);
  • SidebarRail, the strip along the sidebar’s edge that toggles it;
  • a second sidebar on the same page; Ctrl/⌘B toggles every sidebar on the page;
  • in the header placement: sub-menus that drop down from the row (a navigation menu), and a “More” entry gathering the links that do not fit (the row scrolls instead);
  • a sidebar below a header across the whole page (shadcn’s sidebar-16): see One element for a desktop and a phone.

JavaScript

Section titled “JavaScript”

A small Alpine component, slSidebar, does the work: <sl:sidebar-provider> renders as <div class="sidebar-provider" x-data="slSidebar" data-state="expanded">.

  • It needs Alpine, and no Alpine plugin. It writes the cookie itself (a plain cookie, not $persist, which would store JSON in the browser where the server cannot read it). Alpine is included by default; see Alpine.
  • On a desktop it takes popovertarget off the trigger and sets aria-expanded from the state instead: browsers report a popovertarget button as collapsed while its popover is closed, which the sidebar on a desktop always is. Below 768 px it puts it back. It finds the trigger by its aria-controls.
  • Collapsed to icons, it expands the sidebar when a collapsible group’s icon is clicked, and opens the group. Each menu button’s tooltip is a second small Alpine component, slSidebarMenuTooltip, on the tooltip itself; it shares slTooltip’s code.
  • It fires sl-sidebar-toggle on the provider (it bubbles) after the user collapses or expands the sidebar and when the panel opens or closes: detail is {state: 'expanded' | 'collapsed', open, mobile}.
  • Keep your own x-data off <sl:sidebar-provider>: it would replace slSidebar. Put it on an element inside.
